United States Consul-Genera 1 Nnsh, Bangkok, Slam, report:! 
that the cultivation of rubber in Slam bus only recently been

that It will prove highly successful. There Is, however, one 
thing to fear — namely, the new so-called disease, wtiich I bear 
has developed In the Para rubber plantations of the Malay 
Peninsula. I can learn nothing definite about this peet, except 
that It attacks the leaves and Is very destructive. I am in- 
clined to the opinion that it is caused by the larvw of some 
Insect. 

In this connection It may he Interesting to note tw-o of tbe 
rubber producing plants indigenous to Siani. Tbe more im- 
portant of ttiese is the fVrtis ctaslica. so much used iu tbe 
United States for ornamental purposes, and found in large 
quantities In the Siamese Jungle and throughout India and 
Indo-Chtna generally. 

Rubl>er is collected from these trees by the simple proc«*i 
of making longitudinal scarifications in the bark, from whicii 
the coagulated milk is taken in lung strips. It is said that n 
plant six years old will yield 4 pounds of rubl>er annually of 
a quality which could be sold in I»ndon at about 00 cents per 
pound, but this price appears to me to be a trifle exaggerated. 

The other rubber producing plant of known commercial 
value Is a creeper of great size, prol)abIy one of the Crrcola 
(either U. etculeitta or V. elattira), although from certain 
descriptions I nm sometimes Inclined to believe It to be a 
WUIuyhbeia. It Is most dlflicult to nhtnln any reliable informa-

ers, whatever they may be. yield a fair quality of rubber, pro- 
duced by cutting them Into sections 2 or 3 feet long and collect- 
ing the juice, which is subMoincntly lioilcd for a moment in

One of tbe most prominent characteristics of the social history

snsiptlon of natural products has increased, a fact which Is 
easily understood. 

The definite chemical product cannot, in any case, sufllce for

AMERICAN DRUGGIST AND PHARMACEUTICAL RECORD. 



MARYLAND DRUOQISTS OPPOSE LABEL BILLS. 



All ol S<ctioa o( the Drue Trade Unfte to Opposlag L<bclin£ 
BlUi Jolot CoalatacM at All Braoclia of Ibc Trade. 

(Frfim our Regular Corretpondenl.) 
UulUiuore. Februarj' -1- — Munufacturere of pharinaccutlcBls 
and representntlven of the Maryland College of Pbarinncy, the 
Maryland rhuruiaceutical AsMclatlOD and wholesale as well 
■B retail druRglstR aRsembled In one of the parlor* of the Kntaw 
House on the 14tb ioat to protest against the Godwin and the 
Bryan bills now pending In the Legislature. The former pro- 
vides that all proprietory and patent medicines are to have 
the formulas printed upon the wrapper or label, and that any 
romiMuud coutalning more than 8 per cent, of ethyl alcohol or 
more than 1-25 of 1 per cent, of morphine, heroin or cocaine or 
any of their derivative*, or more than ^4 of 1 per cent, of chloral 
hydrate or any quantity of belladonna, cotton root, ergot or 
other abortlfacicui, shall have the fact plainly printed on the 
label In red letters. The Bryan bill, which was drafted by the 
State's Attorney-General after the death of a child from some 
soothing syrup, speclfles that every preparation which contains 
drugs In dangerous qnnntitles shall be labeled " poison." Ad- 
dresRes were made at the meeting by Edward M. Parrislx, of the 
CnfTeeno Company ; Harry Hlnes, of the Enjeri<on Drug Com- 
pany; A. C. Meyer, manufacturer of Dr. Bull's Cough Syrup; 
Dr. A. J. Corning, president of the Baltimore Kctall Druggisu' 
Association; R. El Lee Williamson, of Williamson & Watts, 
and Dr. John 0. Beck, manager of the Calvert Drag Company. 
It was resolved to ask the Lcxi<*latlve Committee on Hygiene 
to set a date for a bearUig at which the arguments of the drag- 
gtets In opposition can be presented. On this occasion two 
delegates from each of the divisions represented at the meeting 
are to go to Annapolis and offer arguments. It was also de- 
termined to raise no money whatever for the purpose of lobby- 
ing against the proposed measures, the druggists being of the 
opinion that the matter ought to be fought out on its own mer- 
its, traiik A. Bally, of James Bally & Son, presided at the 
meeting. 

The bills were also dl-scussed on the 17th Inst, before a meet- 
ing of physicians at McCoy Uall, Johns Hopkins University. The 
medical profession generally favors the measures. State Sen- 
ator J. Charles Lluthlcum presided at this meeting, and the 
speakers were Dr. William S. Thayer and Dr. W. Harvey 
Wiley, from the Department of Agriculture at Washington. 



Rumor* That Standard Oil Is to Enter the Drug Field. 

Rumors are afloat in Chicago that the Standard Oil Com- 
pany Is about to o|)erate actively In drugs and will shortly erect 
a laboratory for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals that will 
rival the great establishment of Parke, Davis & Co» In Detroit 
Efforts m.nde In this city to verify the rumor met with failure. 
When the Bolton Drug Company, of Brooklyn, was interrogated 
In the matter It scoffed at the notion of the thing. Mr. Bol- 
ton was in Chicago last week, the manager of the Bolton Drug 
Company sold, and arranged for the opening of a branch ware- 
house to serve as a distributing center for the preparations 
made and marketed by the United Drug Company, but the 
Standard Oil Company had no relation to the United Drug 
Company. It Is likely that the rumor originated through Mr. 
Bolton's visit to Chicago.

CORJtEI.ITJS P. DOHUE. 

Cornelius P. Dobme, a member of the firm of Sharp & 
Dohme, manufacturers of pharmaceuticals and extracts, at 
Howard and Pratt streets, Baltimore, died on the evening of 
the ir.th Inst, after an Illness of six months. Mr. Dohme was 
born 87 years ago In Germany and came to the United States 
as far back as I8ri2. About 1882 he became a partner of the 
flrni of Sharp & Dohme, which his brother, Louis Dohme, bad 
founded In LSflO, together with A. P. Sharp. In IRfifi another 
brother, Charles E. Dohme, was admitted Into the business. 
The mannfactiire of pbannaccutlcals was then hardly more 
than In Its Infancy, but the Arm recognized its possibilities and 



engaged In the enterprise, with most gratifying success. For 
a number of years Mr. Cornelus P. Dohme was at the bead of 
the pill department, his thoroughness and sound attainments 
being an Important factor in the success of the house. He 
continued active until a sboii time ago. Personally he was of 
a most amiable disposition, w^hicb quality won him a ho«t of 
friends.

Following a fall on the Icy pavement In front of his late

his removal to the University Hospital, where be and Dr. A. C.

for consultation. Every effort was made to prevent bis BinklDg 
under the shock, ns he was over 65 years old. He failed to 
rally, however, and, although given the best medical aoA surgi- 
cal atentloD of the city, he died on February 17. Mr. Dobbins 
was one of the best-known business men in Phlladelpbia. His 
connection with the Wyeth Arm began in 1865, and until rec«nt 
years be took an active part In the conduct of the company. 
He was a member of the Union League and the PblladelphlM 
Country Club and a trnstee of the Philadelphia College of Phar- 
macy.

Stamped Paper in Argentina. 

Minister Beaupr6, of Argentina, forwards to tbe State De- 
partment a copy of a law of that republic regulating tbe tue 
of stamped pai)er and stamps In all commercial transactions, 
which became operative January 1. By this law substantially 
every written contract, document or obligation Is made sub- 
ject to stamp taxes, and where money values are stated tbe 
stamped paper or stamps required are fixed at about one-tenth 
of 1 i)er cent ; that Is to say, on expressed values from $20 to 
$100. 10 cents In stamps; from 9101 to $200, 20 cents In sUmps, 
and so on, the increase t>elng 10 cents for each $100 or frac- 
tion. There are a nimiber of exceptions to this rule, hot tbe 
rate given will apply to nearly all commercial transactions, 
.Vmong the ejcceptions may be noted insurance policies, wblcb 
must be stamped according to tbe prescribed schedule providing 
tbat policies from $100 to $1,000 shall pny 5 cents; on each 
$1,000 np to $5,000. 25 cents: from $."1.1x10 to $10,000 a charge of 
.'iO cent*: above $10,0<Ni iind not above $15,000, 75 cents, and 
from $15,000 to $20,000, $1. .Ml above that must pay for each 
additional $5,000, or a fraction thereof, 25 cents.

A Retail DrwnUt Gives to HU employees Stock Worth 
$350,000. 

C. H. McGonnell, president of the Economical Drug Com- 
pany of Cblcago, bas recently set aside one-fonrtb of tbe 1100,- 
000 of common stock of bis company to be gireu to employees 
who hare been In tbe employ of tbe company for Utc years or 
more. This baa been divided Into lots ranging from 1500 for 
tbe porter to (lO.UOO for tbe manager. As tbe stock pays a 
dividend of -10 per cent., tbe gift Is really worth very macfa 
more than the face value, and according to Wall Street usage 
would be reckoned at ten times tbe face value. While tbe 
stock Is to be turned over to the employees, each one Is ex- 
pected to pay for bis stock at tbe fare value from bis dividends, 
but since only two and a half years would be required to do 
this, this requirement is by no means a hardship. 

Mr. McC'oonell bas built up a most remarkable business In 
tbe fifteen years or so since be established bis store In tbe 
hesrt of the downtown district of Chicago. Owing to the con- 
centratiou of the offices of physicians in tbe center of Chicago 
there are probably 1,000 physicians located within a few blocks 
of his store, and as a result be docs a prescription business 
ranging from 400 to 000 prescriptions a day. lie began with 
the sale of soda waler and cigars, but eventually got rid of 
l>otb of these side lines, believing that they were detrimental 
rather than beneflclal to bis legitimate drug bu.<iinei<s. 

Prior to his undertaking the cstabllshmeut of this com- 
pany he had been engaged in an entirely different line of trade, 
and even now makes no pretense of any knowledge of phar- 
macy. Intrusting all purely pbarmaceatlcal matters to bis ex- 
pert pharmaceutical staff. 

Notwithstanding his purely commercial training be has 
taken a remarkable stand in bis attitude toward patent medi- 
cines. He bas never permitted his employees to endeavor to 
sell anything except what is called for. Most cut rate drug- 
gists Insist upon their salesmen making an effort to substitute 
when cut rate patents are asked for. This Mr. McConnell has 
never permitted In bis establishment. Ue had, however, a dis- 
agreement with one Arm, and when It was officially stated, by 
the United States Government, that a preparation made by this 
drm contained a large percentage of alcohol, he Instructed each 
salesman to state that fact In making sales of that particular 
remedy, and he used bis show windows to advertise tbe fact. 
In the same way he has endeavored to discourage the sale of 
catarrh snuff contuining coi'aitie by wrapping up with each 
bottle of (<uch reniwly a statement of the results of analyseH 
made by the chemist of the Board of Health, and warning the 
purcha»er against the danger incurred by the use of the remedy. 

Mr. McConnell Is a firm believer In having tbe best help 
and paying an adequate remuneration. He has Invariably ad- 
vanced the wages of his clerks from time to time as he thought 
advancement was deserved, without walling to be asked, and by 
giving a certain small commission on amount of sales made 
bas given a B|>ecial incentive to each employee to exert himself 
to the utmost at all times. One result of this liberal policy is 
shown in tbe fart that the number of sales made by each of 
bin salesmen exceed by 25 to 50 per cent, the number of sales 
made by men employed in the same capacity in other stores of 
tbe same character. His latest move In giving his employees 
one-fourth of the common stock of tbe company Is exactly In 
line with his previous record as an employer. 

.Mr. McConnelTs health has of late not been particularly 
robust, aud be sailed from New York last week for a seven 
months' tour through the West Indies and Central America. He 
has taken long vacations every summer during the last four or 
five years and finds that the loyalty of his employees Is such 
that his business never suffers by bis absence.

Stelnkopff sold his share of the bu-Hlnoss in 185)7 to the late

The discoverer of radium met with bis death on April 20

Gautbler-Vlllars, a scleiitlflc publisher on tbe Qual dcs Grands- 
Augustlns and was crossing tbe Rue Dauphlne when be was

passed over his bead, and death was Instantaneous. Tbe driver 
was arrested, bat acquitted, as It seemed evident that M. Curie 
bad been bidden from his view by a cab and only came Into 
view at tbe very moment the accident occurred. 

The news was broken to the savant's father, and Madame 
Curie, who was absent from Paris, was sent for. It will t>e re- 
membered that this lady took a leading part In tbe now his- 
torical series of experiments by which radium was discovered. 
They were n very united and unassamlug couple, to whom pub- 
licity of uny kind wns always distasteful, and altboush tbe 
French Government would certainly have honored the late 
savant by a public funeral, Mndnuie Curie's one rcqucot. tu be

Born in Paris. .May 15, 1850, Pierre Curie was counted among

Tbe Irony of fate was i>erhap« never more tragically evident 
than In tlie case of this gifle*! and worthy couple. Alnwst the 
whole of their married life was one long stmggle, carrying out
